related_questions.question: How do you treat a hematoma on your scalp?

text_blocks.snippet: Scalp hematoma treatment depends on its severity. Simple, mild hematomas can be treated with the R.I.C.E. method (rest, ice, compression, and elevation) and over-the-counter pain relievers. More serious hematomas may require drainage, either through a needle (aspiration) or surgery (craniotomy or burr holes).
snippet_highlighted_words: Simple, mild hematomas can be treated with the R.I.C.E.
method (rest, ice, compression, and elevation) and over-the-counter pain relievers

list.title: R.I.C.E. Method:
list.snippet: For minor hematomas, rest the injured area, apply ice packs (wrapped in a towel to prevent frostbite) for 15-20 minutes at a time, compress the area with a bandage, and elevate the injured part above the heart.

list.title: Over-the-counter pain relievers:
list.snippet: Medications like acetaminophen or ibuprofen can help manage pain and swelling.

list.title: Aspiration:
list.snippet: In some cases, a doctor may use a needle to drain the pooled blood from the hematoma.

list.title: Surgery:
list.snippet: More severe hematomas, particularly those causing neurological issues, may require surgery to remove the hematoma. This can involve creating burr holes (small holes in the skull) or a craniotomy (removing a section of the skull).

list.title: Medications:
list.snippet: Depending on the cause and severity, medications may be used to manage blood pressure, clotting issues, or other related problems.

list.title: Aspirin:
list.snippet: Avoid aspirin for hematoma treatment as it can increase bleeding, according to Verywell Health.

list.title: Scalp Hematomas in Infants:
list.snippet: In infants, most scalp hematomas resolve on their own, but some may require interventions like hemorrhoidectomy or aspiration to prevent complications.

list.title: Intracranial Hematomas:
list.snippet: Intracranial hematomas (those within the skull) can be serious and may require immediate surgical intervention to prevent neurological damage, according to the Mayo Clinic.

list.title: Observation:
list.snippet: Some hematomas, especially small ones without symptoms, may only require close observation and monitoring for any changes in neurological status.

related_questions.question: How long does it take for a scalp hematoma to go away?

text_blocks.snippet: A scalp hematoma, or a collection of blood under the scalp, typically takes a few weeks to several months to resolve on its own. The exact time frame depends on the size and severity of the hematoma. Minor hematomas may resolve within a couple of weeks, while larger ones can take months to fully disappear.
snippet_highlighted_words: a few weeks to several months

list.snippet: Minor hematomas: These may resolve within a few days to a couple of weeks.
Larger or deeper hematomas: These can take several weeks to a few months to fully heal.
Cephalohematoma (in newborns): This type of scalp hematoma, often caused by birth trauma, can take weeks to months to resolve.
Calcification: In some cases, a cephalohematoma may begin to harden or calcify as it heals, which is a normal part of the process.
Impact of size and location: The location and size of the hematoma will influence the healing time.

Treatment: Most scalp hematomas don't require specific treatment and resolve on their own, but a doctor should be consulted if there are signs of infection or if the hematoma is not resolving as expected, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

related_questions.question: Is a scalp hematoma bad?
related_questions.snippet: When you fall or hit your head, you may get a large bump on the head that can look serious. But a scalp hematoma, or goose egg, is usually not a sign of brain damage. However, some head injuries are serious.
related_questions.title: Head Bumps: From Minor Goose Eggs to Serious Brain Injuries

text_blocks.snippet: A scalp hematoma, a collection of blood under the scalp, can often be treated with conservative measures like the RICE method (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) for minor injuries. However, larger or severe hematomas may require medical intervention, including drainage or surgery.
snippet_highlighted_words: RICE method (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) for minor injuries

list.title: RICE Method:
list.snippet: Rest the affected area, apply ice packs wrapped in a cloth for 15-20 minutes at a time to reduce swelling, compress the area with a bandage (avoiding excessive pressure), and elevate the head if possible to minimize blood pooling.

list.title: Pain Relief:
list.snippet: Over-the-counter pain relievers like acetaminophen can help with discomfort, but avoid aspirin or ibuprofen as they can increase bleeding.

list.title: Observation:
list.snippet: Monitor the hematoma for changes in size or appearance. If symptoms worsen, seek medical attention.
Severe Headache: A persistent or worsening headache could indicate a serious head injury.
Loss of Consciousness: Any loss of consciousness, even brief, requires immediate medical evaluation.
Neurological Symptoms: Confusion, drowsiness, vision changes, seizures, or difficulty moving should be addressed promptly.
Increasing Pain or Swelling: If the hematoma continues to grow or become more painful, it may require drainage.
Suspected Brain Injury: Any suspicion of a brain injury warrants immediate medical care.

list.title: Surgical Drainage:
list.snippet: For large hematomas, a doctor may need to drain the blood to relieve pressure on the brain or other tissues.

list.title: Craniotomy:
list.snippet: In some cases, a craniotomy (removal of a section of skull) may be necessary to access and remove the hematoma.

list.title: Burr Holes:
list.snippet: A less invasive procedure involves drilling small holes in the skull to drain the hematoma.

list.title: Follow Medical Advice:
list.snippet: Always adhere to your doctor's instructions regarding treatment and follow-up care.

list.title: Avoid Alcohol:
list.snippet: Alcohol can thin the blood and increase the risk of bleeding, so it should be avoided after a head injury.

list.title: Monitor for Changes:
list.snippet: Be vigilant for any new or worsening symptoms, and seek medical help if needed.
